blocks.text: At a bank in Ibadan, customers are served in the order they arrived — that is a queue, and it is what everyone considers fair. On the same counter sits a tray of forms where the clerk always picks up whichever was placed last — that is a stack, and it is exactly what your processor does with function calls. Two structures, one difference: which end you remove from.

blocks.markdown:
## Abstract data types, not implementations

A stack and a queue are **abstract data types**: they are defined by an interface and a behavioural contract, not by a representation. Both can be built over an array or a linked list, and both offer $O(1)$ operations when built correctly.

The discipline is the whole definition:

- A **stack** is **LIFO** — last in, first out. Insertion and removal happen at the same end, called the top.
- A **queue** is **FIFO** — first in, first out. Insertion happens at the rear and removal at the front.

Deliberately restricting the interface is the point. Because a stack exposes no indexing, its invariants are trivial to reason about and its implementation can be swapped freely.

blocks.caption: A priority queue is included for contrast: it is the one member of the family whose operations are not constant time.

blocks.title: Abstract data type
blocks.text: A specification of a set of values together with the operations on them, stated in terms of observable behaviour and independent of any representation. A *data structure* is a concrete representation that implements an ADT. "Stack" is an ADT; "array-backed stack with a top index" is a data structure.

blocks.markdown:
### Implementing a stack

Over an array, keep an integer `top` holding the index of the next free slot. `push` writes at `top` and increments; `pop` decrements and reads. Both are $O(1)$, and with a doubling buffer `push` is $O(1)$ amortised. Over a singly linked list, push and pop at the head — both $O(1)$ worst case, at the cost of a pointer per element and poor locality.

Either way, the two error conditions must be handled explicitly: `pop` or `peek` on an empty stack is an **underflow**, and `push` onto a full fixed-capacity stack is an **overflow**.

The call stack is the canonical instance. Each call pushes an activation record and each return pops one, and the LIFO discipline is exactly what makes recursion work: the most recently suspended call is always the next to resume.

### Implementing a queue: the circular buffer

A naive array queue with a moving `front` and `rear` leaks capacity — after $c$ enqueues and $c$ dequeues, `rear` has reached the end of the array while every slot is free. The fix is to let the indices **wrap**:

```
enqueue(v):
    if count == capacity: grow or reject
    buffer[rear] = v
    rear  = (rear + 1) mod capacity
    count = count + 1

dequeue():
    if count == 0: underflow
    v     = buffer[front]
    front = (front + 1) mod capacity
    count = count - 1
    return v
```

With $c$ slots there are $c + 1$ possible occupancies but only $c$ distinct values of $(\text{rear} - \text{front}) \bmod c$, so index comparison alone cannot distinguish full from empty — both give $\text{front} = \text{rear}$. Hence the explicit `count` above. The alternative is to sacrifice one slot and declare the buffer full at $c - 1$ elements.

blocks.title: Evaluating a postfix expression with a stack
blocks.prompt: Evaluate the reverse Polish expression 5 3 2 * + 4 - using a single stack, showing the stack contents after each token.

steps.text: Rule: an operand is pushed; an operator pops two operands, applies itself, and pushes the result. Critically, the *first* value popped is the **right-hand** operand, which matters for the non-commutative operators $-$ and $/$.
Token `3` → push. Stack: [5, 3]. Token `2` → push. Stack: [5, 3, 2].
Token `4` → push. Stack: [11, 4]. Token `-` → pop 4 (right), pop 11 (left), push $11 - 4$. Stack: [7].

Input is exhausted and the stack holds exactly one value, which is the result. Two validity checks fall out of the trace: an operator finding fewer than two operands means the expression is malformed, and more than one value left at the end means the same. The equivalent infix expression is $5 + 3 \times 2 - 4$, and postfix needs no parentheses because token order alone fixes the grouping.

items: **Stack — call management.** Each invocation pushes an activation record; each return pops one. Unbounded recursion exhausts the region and raises a stack overflow.
**Stack — delimiter matching.** Push each opening bracket, pop and compare on each closing one. Acceptance also requires the stack to be empty at end of input, otherwise `([` is wrongly accepted.
**Stack — expression handling.** Postfix evaluation as above, and Dijkstra's shunting-yard algorithm for converting infix to postfix.
**Stack — depth-first search.** A LIFO frontier drives the traversal along one branch until it dead-ends.
**Stack — undo.** The most recent action must be the first reversed, which is the LIFO contract exactly.
**Queue — breadth-first search.** A FIFO frontier finishes distance $d$ before starting distance $d+1$, which is why BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
**Queue — scheduling and buffering.** Round-robin CPU scheduling, print spooling, and producer–consumer pipelines all require arrival order to be preserved.

blocks.title: The frontier's discipline *is* the traversal
blocks.text: Breadth-first and depth-first search are the same algorithm; the only difference is whether the frontier is a queue or a stack. If you can state that sentence and justify it, you understand both algorithms and both ADTs.

blocks.title: Check emptiness before you remove
blocks.text: `pop` and `dequeue` are partial operations — they have a precondition. Silently returning a sentinel such as 0 or −1 on an empty container hides the error at the point where it can still be diagnosed and surfaces it much later as a wrong answer. Either raise, or return an explicit optional the caller must unwrap.

points: A stack is LIFO with insertion and removal at one end; a queue is FIFO with insertion at the rear and removal at the front.
Both are abstract data types: the contract is the definition, and array or linked implementations are interchangeable.
All stack and queue operations are $O(1)$; a priority queue is the exception at $O(\log n)$ with a binary heap.
A circular buffer advances indices modulo the capacity, which prevents a queue from drifting off the end of its array.
Full and empty give the same index configuration, so an explicit count or one sacrificed slot is required.
Postfix evaluation pushes operands and applies operators to the top two, with the first value popped being the right-hand operand.
A queue frontier yields breadth-first search and a stack frontier yields depth-first search — otherwise the algorithms are identical.
